title: Fold Paper 42 Times and It Would Reach the Moon 🌕
description:
If you could fold an ordinary sheet of paper in half 42 times, it would be thick enough to reach past the Moon. But try it yourself and you'll get stuck at about seven.

Every fold doubles the thickness. A normal sheet is about 0.1 mm thick: 10 folds make about 10 cm, 23 folds make about 839 m (taller than the tallest building on Earth, 828 m), and 42 folds make about 440,000 km, past the Moon's average distance of 384,400 km. So why can't you keep going? Each fold also halves the sheet, and the curved edge of every fold uses up more and more paper: each new fold needs about four times the length. In 2002 a high-school student set the record of 12 folds, using a strip of paper about 1.2 km (4,000 ft) long.

How many times can you fold a sheet? Tell us below.

More true whys: https://www.youtube.com/@truewhys?sub_confirmation=1

Sources: Scientific American (P. Plait, how many paper folds would get you to the Moon); Guinness World Records (most times to fold a piece of paper, 27 Jan 2002) and its 2025 article; Science News (Folding Paper in Half Twelve Times); NASA (Moon distance); Burj Khalifa official height.
